narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 91.9% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process uses this prediction to assess risk, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by your academic performance during law school. Your first-year and third-year class rankings were the two strongest factors pushing the model toward predicting failure. Both placed you in the bottom decile of your class—far below the average of roughly the 6th decile among students who were accepted. These low rankings signaled to the model a consistent pattern of struggling relative to your peers, which strongly increased the estimated risk of failing the bar.

Your LSAT score was the third most important factor, but it worked in the opposite direction. At 37, it sits almost exactly at the average of accepted students and therefore slightly pulled the prediction toward success. Unfortunately, this positive influence was not large enough to overcome the much stronger negative signals from your class rankings.

Given these results, you should focus on improving your academic performance if you retake courses or enroll elsewhere. Strengthening your class standing would likely have the biggest impact on future predictions. Consider seeking academic support, adjusting study strategies, or exploring schools with different grading curves before reapplying. This targeted improvement gives you the clearest path to a more favorable outcome next time.
